https://travelandtannins.com/workers-dri.text: Destinations Workers Drilling in Romania Broke Into a Cave Sealed for 5.5 Million Years — and Found an Entire Living World That Has Never Seen the Sun By Adeline Vance August 3, 2026 Source: Wikipedia Almost everything alive on the surface of this planet runs, ultimately, on sunlight. Plants capture light and turn it into sugar. Animals eat the plants. Other animals eat those animals. Pull the sun out of that equation and nearly every food chain we know collapses within a season. For most of scientific history, this was treated as a basic rule of biology: life needs the sun, if not directly then a few steps removed. Then, in 1986, workers in southeastern Romania were drilling exploratory boreholes near the Black Sea coast, scouting ground for a proposed power plant. What they found instead was a hole leading down into a cave system that had been sealed off from the outside world for something on the order of five and a half million years, since long before our species existed. The air inside was toxic. There was no light, and there never had been. By every expectation, it should have been an empty stone tomb. Instead, researchers who descended into it found a thriving, complex, interconnected community of living creatures, dozens of species that exist nowhere else on Earth, surviving in permanent darkness on an energy source that has nothing to do with the sun. Here is the story of Movile Cave, the sealed world beneath Romania. An Accidental Doorway Source: Wikipedia The discovery was pure chance. In the mid-1980s, crews working near the port city of Mangalia, on Romania’s Black Sea coast, were drilling test holes to evaluate the ground for construction. The landscape above gives away nothing: scrubby, dusty farmland, flat and unremarkable, with no dramatic sinkhole or cave mouth to suggest that anything unusual lies beneath. Nobody had any reason to think there was a hidden world under their feet. But the drilling broke through into a void, and that void turned out to be the entrance to a maze-like network of flooded limestone passages roughly eighteen meters, or about sixty feet, below the surface. Sealed above by thick layers of clay and limestone, the cave had no meaningful connection to the surface world. Rainwater did not seep in. Surface air did not circulate down. The system had been effectively closed since the late Miocene epoch, when the geology of the region shifted and shut the door. When scientists began exploring and studying it, they realized very quickly that this was not an ordinary cave. It was something far rarer: a sealed environment that had been running its own biological experiment, undisturbed, for millions of years, and had been opened by accident. Like our content? Follow us for more. Proving It Was Really Sealed Source: Wikipedia An obvious question hangs over any claim like this. How can anyone be confident that a cave was truly cut off, that nothing had been trickling in from the surface across all that time? Caves leak. Water finds its way through rock. The assertion that this system had been isolated for millions of years is an extraordinary one, and it needed extraordinary support. Researchers found an elegant way to test it, and the timing was almost too convenient. The Chernobyl reactor accident occurred in 1986, the same year the cave was discovered, and it spread detectable radioactive isotopes across large areas of Europe, including Romanian soil. Those isotopes became a kind of chemical timestamp on surface water. So scientists tested the water inside the cave for the telltale radioactive signatures of that fallout, and found none of it. Not a trace. Whatever water was down in the cave had not come from the surface, not recently and apparently not for a very long time. It was a striking confirmation that the seal was real: one of the most widely dispersed contamination events in modern history had not penetrated a single drop into this underground world. Combined with the geology and the peculiar chemistry of the cave’s water and air, the evidence pointed to a system that had been closed off since roughly five and a half million years ago. The Air That Would Not Sustain Us Source: Wikimedia Commons Movile Cave is not a place a person can casually visit, and not only because access is tightly restricted and permitted only for approved researchers. The environment inside is deeply hostile to human physiology. The atmosphere in the deeper parts of the system bears very little resemblance to the air at the surface. Oxygen levels run at roughly half of what our lungs expect. Carbon dioxide is present at concentrations enormously higher than in the outside atmosphere. The air is laced with hydrogen sulfide, the compound responsible for the smell of rotten eggs, and with methane and ammonia. The water in the cave’s pools is warm, murky, low in oxygen, and thick with dissolved chemicals. Researchers who have worked there describe an atmosphere that is acrid and pungent, an environment humans can tolerate only briefly and only with careful precautions. Everything about it reads as inhospitable, the sort of chemistry that appears on a list of reasons a place should be lifeless. And yet those same chemicals turn out to be precisely the reason the cave is not lifeless at all. What makes the air unbreathable for us is the fuel that keeps everything down there alive. A Food Chain Built on Chemistry Source: Wikipedia The key to Movile Cave is a process called chemosynthesis. Instead of bacteria and plants harvesting energy from light, the microbes at the base of this ecosystem pull energy from chemical reactions, oxidizing compounds like sulfide, methane, and ammonium to build the organic material that everything else depends on. These bacteria form pale, slimy microbial mats that float on the surface of the water and coat the cave walls near the pools. Those mats are the pasture of this underground world. From there, the food web assembles itself much as it would anywhere else, just without a single photon involved. Small creatures graze the microbial mats. Larger creatures eat the grazers. Predators sit at the top. The whole structure, from the bottom up, is powered by chemistry drawn out of rock and water rather than by sunlight falling on leaves. What made this so significant scientifically is that when Movile was studied, ecosystems running independently of the sun were known essentially from one place: the deep-sea hydrothermal vents discovered on mid-ocean ridges in the late 1970s. Movile added a second, radically different example, a freshwater, land-based version sealed inside continental limestone rather than perched on the ocean floor. It was, as researchers have described it, the first such subterranean ecosystem ever found, and it forced textbook diagrams of how life on Earth is powered to be redrawn. The Creatures in the Dark Source: Wikipedia The inhabitants of Movile Cave read like the cast of a science fiction story. Surveys have identified somewhere around fifty invertebrate species living in the system, and the striking figure is how many of them exist nowhere else: depending on the survey and the year, roughly thirty-three to thirty-seven of them are endemic, found only in this one cave. They have been evolving in isolation, in the dark, for millions of years, and it shows. The roster includes spiders, pseudoscorpions, woodlice, centipedes, leeches, snails, water scorpions, and a range of smaller organisms whose classification researchers are still working out. Certain features recur again and again across otherwise unrelated creatures. Most of them are blind, many having lost functional eyes entirely, because eyes are an expensive organ to maintain and useless in a place that has never had light. Most of them are also unpigmented, pale or translucent, since coloration serves little purpose where nothing can be seen. A water scorpion has abandoned eyes altogether. A blind leech swims in water no sunbeam has ever touched. A centipede with serrated hind legs was nicknamed the king of the cave by the scientists who described it. Each of these species is a small demonstration of what evolution does when you remove light from the equation and leave the process running for a few million years. Why This Cave Matters Beyond the sheer strangeness of it, Movile Cave has become important to science in its own right, and its significance reaches well past Romania. The cave functions as a natural laboratory for studying how life copes with extreme conditions, and researchers have used it to explore questions ranging from evolutionary biology to microbiology to the chemistry of how organisms process toxic compounds. Its most intriguing role may be in the search for life elsewhere. An ecosystem that thrives in permanent darkness, in a chemically harsh environment, powered entirely by reactions in rock and water, is a reasonable model for what life might look like beneath the ice of certain moons in our own solar system, or below the surface of Mars. If life exists in such places, it will not be sunbathing; it will be doing something much closer to what the microbes of Movile do. That makes this cave one of the better analogs available for thinking about biology beyond Earth, and it has attracted research interest on exactly those grounds. Access to the cave remains strictly limited, which is entirely appropriate: this is a fragile system that survived untouched for millions of years and could be disrupted easily by careless visitation. There is something humbling in the whole affair. A crew drilling a routine borehole in an unremarkable field opened a door onto a world that had been sealed since before our species existed, and inside was a complete, functioning community of life that broke one of biology’s assumed rules. It is a reminder that the planet is not finished revealing itself, that discoveries of real consequence can still turn up under a dusty patch of farmland, and that life is substantially more inventive about where and how it survives than we tend to assume. Somewhere beneath the Romanian countryside, in absolute darkness, that ancient experiment is still running. Like our content? Follow us for more. https://cphpost.dk/2026-09-30/news/round.text: Air traffic at two Polish airports was briefly suspended Wednesday morning as military aircraft operated in Polish airspace during Russian attacks on Ukraine. Poland’s aviation authority, PANSA, said flights at Lublin and Rzeszów airports were suspended before resuming at 7:10 a.m. Poland’s military operational command, RSZ, said it had activated forces including ground-based air defense systems and radar surveillance. “These measures are preventive in nature and are intended to secure and protect the airspace, particularly in areas bordering the threatened regions,” RSZ said. Poland borders Ukraine, where Russian attacks overnight killed at least three people and injured seven in and around Kyiv, according to local officials cited by Reuters. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were killed and four injured in the capital. Fires damaged private homes, a shop and a warehouse. Kyiv regional governor Timur Tkachenko said a child was killed and three people injured in the surrounding region, where homes, warehouses and cars were hit. There were also reports of Ukrainian attacks inside Russia. Private homes were reportedly damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Samara region, according to regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev. The region, about 1,100 kilometers southeast of Moscow, is an important oil-producing area. Reuters said it could not independently verify the reports. Travelers going between Copenhagen Central Station and Næstved by way of Køge face longer travel times until 1:00 p.m. on Wednesday. DSB, the Danish national rail operator, announced the problem on its website. A few trains that usually run on the line through Køge Nord are taking a detour through Roskilde instead. These trains will not make any stops between Copenhagen Central Station and Ringsted. To help travelers get to their destinations, buses are running between Køge and Næstved to replace the missing train service. The delay is due to a signal problem at Kildebronde in East Zealand. Banedanmark, the state agency in charge of railway infrastructure, told Ritzau, the Danish news agency, that a severed cable caused the signal failure. DSB told passengers to check Rejseplanen, the national travel planning service, before leaving home. Fewer trains were already running between Odense and Fredericia before this latest problem, and that reduction will last through Sunday, October 18. DSB stated that this date is an estimate, and the issues could end earlier or later than expected. All regional trains on this route have been replaced by buses since Friday, when a fire started in an equipment hut near the town of Aarup on western Funen. International trains, along with InterCity and InterCityLyn express trains, are running on their normal schedules, but they must move at lower speeds on parts of the route. All train traffic between Odense and Fredericia stopped for about two hours on Tuesday afternoon after a cable fell onto the tracks and short-circuited an overhead power line. A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions. Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh. Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament. Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken. “As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper. Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark. The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed. The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well. However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament. During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion. Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings. “I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper. She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position. Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview. However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea. “It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken. Denmark’s minister for homeland security and emergency preparedness, Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, says there is a clear need to talk with members of the Danish parliament about how to protect the country against cyberattacks. Bech-Nielsen belongs to SF (Socialistisk Folkeparti), the Socialist People’s Party, which is a left-wing and green political party in Denmark. She spoke about the situation to the Danish broadcaster TV 2. “The serious threat assessment and recent events are the reason why I have summoned the parties to a discussion of what initiatives can be set in motion,” she said. The minister called the political parties in the Danish parliament, to discuss what specific steps Denmark should take to make its digital systems safer. The statement did not say when this meeting will take place. Her comments came right after Sund & Bælt, the state-owned company in charge of major Danish bridge and tunnel links, announced on Tuesday afternoon that its construction site at Rødbyhavn was hit by what it called a cyber incident. “Our contractor, FLC, has informed us that they have been subjected to a cyber incident,” said Jens Villemoes, the head of press at Sund & Bælt, in a statement published on the company’s website. FLC stands for Femern Link Contractors, the consortium hired to build the tunnel. The local newspaper Lolland-Falsters Folketidende described the event as a hacker attack. According to the newspaper, the problems meant that workers were ordered not to connect to Wi-Fi, turn on their computers, or open emails from the contractor. Large parts of the computer network were shut down. The security guards could not use their digital access systems, and employees were unable to log their working hours in the normal way. The problems also spread to work on the water. Several ships had to stop moving because they lost access to their digital tools and data. According to the newspaper, these issues first began during the night leading up to Monday. Bech-Nielsen had actually called for the political meeting before the problems hit the Femern project. That decision came after a recent leak of Danish CPR numbers, which are the personal identification numbers assigned to all citizens in Denmark. The minister said it is still too early to draw final conclusions about the latest incident, but noted that “the authorities are investigating” it. King Frederik and Queen Mary will welcome Vietnamese President To Lam and his wife, Ngo Phuong Ly, for a three-day state visit from October 19 to 21. The Danish Royal House has published the official program, which includes cultural visits, political meetings and events in Copenhagen. The presidential couple will arrive at Copenhagen Airport on Monday before joining the Danish royals for a wreath-laying ceremony at Kastellet and a carriage ride to Amalienborg Palace. Their first day includes visits to Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, a public library, the Court Theatre and the Niels Bohr Institute. A gala banquet at Christiansborg Palace will follow. On Tuesday, Frederik and To Lam will attend a business conference hosted by Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main business and employers’ association. Meanwhile, Ngo Phuong Ly will visit Copenhagen Contemporary to see an exhibition featuring eight artists connected to Greenland. Queen Mary will later join her for lunch at Gro Spiseri, a rooftop greenhouse restaurant in Østerbro. To Lam will also meet Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, while the presidential couple will meet Vietnamese residents in Denmark. Tuesday concludes with a concert event at the Glyptoteket museum. On Wednesday, Frederik and To Lam will take a boat tour of Copenhagen Harbour, including views of the Lynetteholm peninsula. The visit concludes at Amalienborg at 11 a.m. Denmark and Vietnam mark 55 years of diplomatic relations this year. Frederik and Mary last visited Vietnam officially in 2022, when they were crown prince and crown princess. To Lam serves as both Vietnam’s president and general secretary of its ruling Communist Party. A woman from Struer has set a national longevity record, reaching 112 years and 218 days on Wednesday and surpassing the previous record held by Karla Lindholm Jensen. Schwalbe also joins the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people. The world’s oldest living person is Britain’s Ethel Caterham, who is 117. The previous Danish record holder, Karla Lindholm Jensen from Herning, died in 2020. Ahead of the milestone, Jyllands-Posten attempted to interview Schwalbe, but she needed a day of rest. Instead, the newspaper spoke with two of her three daughters. Her daughter Hanne Jensen, 86, described how her mother sometimes struggles to understand that her children are now elderly themselves. “She knows well enough that we are getting older, but she forgets that we can no longer withstand everything,” Jensen told the newspaper. Schwalbe was born in Salling in 1914, just months before World War I began, and grew up alongside nine siblings. She married her first husband in 1938, and the couple had three children. Despite her age, Schwalbe continues to live in her own home in Struer. Her life has previously been documented by regional broadcaster TV Midtvest in the television series “Kirstens vilde år,” which airs on TV 2. Schwalbe has attributed her longevity partly to genetics. Four of her nine siblings also lived beyond 100, she told Berlingske in 2024. She has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a positive outlook, previously telling TV Midtvest that a person’s mood plays an important role in living a long life. Rising numbers of serious traffic injuries have prompted Moderaterne, the Moderates, to call for stricter safety rules for people using electric bicycles. Sten Larsen, the party’s health spokesperson, told regional broadcaster TV2 Østjylland that helmets should become a legal requirement for e-bike riders. “E-bikes are both heavier and faster than regular bicycles,” Larsen said. He pointed to an increase in serious injuries and deaths involving electric bicycles as justification for the proposal. Currently, Denmark does not require helmets for ordinary bicycles or standard e-bikes, whose motors provide assistance at speeds of up to 25 kilometers per hour. However, helmets are already mandatory for speed pedelecs, which can provide motor assistance up to 45 kilometers per hour. According to the Danish Road Directorate, 200 e-bike riders were injured in traffic accidents in 2025, including 133 who suffered serious injuries. Another 11 riders died. The number of seriously injured e-bike riders was the highest recorded in six years. Larsen wants to discuss the proposed legislation with Transport Minister Signe Munk of Socialistisk Folkeparti, the Socialist People’s Party. Ritzau sought a comment from Munk, but her ministry said she was unavailable. Cyklistforbundet, the Danish Cyclists’ Federation, opposes making helmets compulsory, arguing that such a measure could discourage cycling. “Our purpose is to get more people to cycle. So every measure that pulls in the opposite direction, we will oppose. But we warmly recommend that people use a bicycle helmet,” federation chair Jens Peter Hansen told TV2 Østjylland. The proposal would introduce a helmet requirement for standard e-bikes, bringing their rules closer to those already applying to faster electric bicycles. Denmark should maintain its current foreign aid budget but change where the money goes, according to Jacob Jensen, foreign affairs spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party. Jensen told Ritzau that his party wants to continue spending 0.7 percent of gross national income on development aid annually. However, he wants more funding directed toward four or five North African countries facing migration pressures toward Europe. The money would come from aid currently allocated to regions including the Caribbean, South America and Southeast Asia. Jensen argued that providing education and employment opportunities could discourage young people from attempting dangerous Mediterranean crossings. “If we can give the typically young men, who alternatively throw themselves into a rubber dinghy across the Mediterranean, a perspective, a job, an education in that area, we can solve many things at once,” he said. Jensen estimated that between 3 billion and 3.5 billion DKK could be redirected. However, the regions he identified were already outside Denmark’s ten largest aid recipients in 2025, when the country distributed 22.9 billion DKK in development aid. Jensen wants to discuss revising Denmark’s development strategy with Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates party. The government’s proposed aid priorities for 2027 through 2030 already include measures to reduce irregular migration. Before the general election, Venstre proposed cutting development aid to 0.5 percent of national income to free approximately 6.5 billion DKK for welfare. That proposal was dropped during government negotiations. Jensen said the proposed reduction was intended to finance other priorities, not reduce development aid as an objective. Greenland’s three governing parties have agreed to support a proposal that would move the territory back to UTC-3 in 2028, reversing a decision made just a few years ago. The parties, which hold a majority in Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, announced their position during a debate Tuesday, according to Sermitsiaq. The proposal would also abolish daylight saving time starting next year. “We have decided that we should return to UTC-3 on the basis of the many people who have submitted a consultation response,” the governing parties said. Sokan nagyon rossz állapotban kerülnek be az ellátórendszerbe: Magyarországon 5 évvel kevesebb a születéskor várható élettartam, mint az európai átlag, de Észak-Magyarországon még 5 évvel kevesebb. Különösen aggasztó, hogy a kezelhető okokból bekövetkezett halálozások számában sereghajtók vagyunk az EU-ban: százezer főre vetítve Magyarországnál csak Romániában, Bulgáriában és Litvániában rosszabb a helyzet. V3 = visegrádi országok; S3 = skandináv országok; EU6 = EU-alapító országok – Forrás: Egyensúly Intézet 2, A betegek csak bolyonganak a rendszerben Magyarországon a betegútnak nincs felelőse, nincs, aki koordinálná a folyamatokat. „És itt nemcsak az ellátórendszert kellene koordinálni, hanem magát a beteget is” – mondta Filippov Gábor. Bizonyos országokban az úgynevezett betegút-koordinátorok segítik a betegeket a diagnózis utáni eligazodásban, például a gyógyszer kiváltásában, a következő kontrollvizsgálaton való részvételben. A szervezés átgondolatlansága nemcsak logisztikai, hanem finanszírozási kérdés is. Fontos szemléletbeli kérdés, hogy az egészségügyi rendszer mit finanszíroz: a gyógyulást, a betegutat, vagyis a teljes folyamatot, vagy csak az egyes eseményeket (például műtéteket). 3, Nincs összehangolva az állami és a magánegészségügy Az emberek a rosszul működő közegészségügyi szolgáltatásokat végül zsebből próbálják meg kifizetni. Filippov Gábor szerint ez régóta fennálló jelenség, generációkon átívelő szocializáció: „Megpróbálok valahogy kontrollt szerezni a sorsom felett, mert azt látom, hogy ha ráhagyom magam az állami intézményrendszerre, akkor el fogok veszni, meg fogok halni, rengeteg baj fog történni.” A szektorsemleges finanszírozás lényege, hogy a társadalombiztosítás attól függetlenül kifizeti valakinek a gyógyulását, hogy az állami vagy magánkórház. Ehhez azonban több előfeltétel szükséges. 4, Szinte összehasonlíthatatlanul keveset költ az állam, mi annál többet Magyarország régiós és EU-s szinten is nagyon keveset költ az egészségügyre a GDP arányában. A saját zsebből fizetett hozzájárulás az összes egészségügyi kiadáshoz viszonyítva viszont kiugróan magas nálunk. Míg sok szakpolitikai kérdésben igaz, hogy nem az a baj, hogy keveset költ az állam, hanem az, hogy nem hatékonyan (például az oktatás esetében), az egészségügynél nem ez a helyzet: az EU-n belül tényleg az egyik legkevesebbet költjük az egészségügyi ellátórendszerre. Óriási probléma az általános, a rendszer minden szintjét érintő humánerőforrás-hiány is: sok kórházi osztály bezárása elsősorban nem az orvoshiány, hanem a szakdolgozók hiánya miatt következik be. 5, A háziorvosi rendszer máshol nem így néz ki A fejlettebb egészségügyi rendszerekre nem az a fajta háziorvosipraxis-méret jellemző, mint ami nálunk, mondta Filippov Gábor. Ennél jobban működő rendszer, amikor többféle szakmát összefogó csoportpraxisokat alakítanak ki, amik a prevencióra, az egészség-magatartás fejlesztésére, az egészségtámogatásra fókuszálnak. Például a háziorvos mellett dietetikus, gyerekpszichológus, pszichiáter, nőgyógyász is dolgozik, akik célzottan tudják kezelni az odalátogató betegeket. „Ma egy háziorvos, az szociális munkás, dietetikus, pszichiáter, minden a világon. Neki kell mindent ellátnia: ez a része is túl medikalizált az alapellátásnak.” 6, Nem csak az egyéni egészségünk miatt fontos az ellátórendszer jövőjének kérdése Magyarországon a társadalom fogy és egyre idősödik. „Ha nem vigyázunk azokra az emberekre, akik itt élnek, ha nem segítjük, hogy minél tovább egészségben éljenek, nemcsak az ország fogy el, hanem a saját közvetlen környezetünk tragédiáival is naponta szembesülünk” – mondta az adásban Boros Tamás. Az egészségügy az ország hosszú távú egészsége mellett a termelékenység növekedése szempontjából is kulcskérdés. Filippov Gábor szerint ahhoz, hogy a tudásunkat növeljük, az egészségben töltött életéveink számát is növelni kell.
